svg.title: Self-attention with trainable Q, K, V weight matrices, building the context vector z squared step by step, with a worked example traced through each step.
svg.desc: Five steps top to bottom: inputs, projection into query/key/value via three learned weight matrices (dk reduced to 2 for readability), scaled dot-product scores, softmax weights, and weighted sum over the value vectors giving context vector z squared = 0.36, 0.60.
svg.text: Self-attention with trainable Q, K, V for x⁽²⁾ (“journey”)
Same flow as before, but weight matrices now sit in front of it — building context vector z⁽²⁾
Each token is a 3-number vector. The example below traces the query x⁽²⁾ meeting x⁽⁵⁾ (“one”).
Step 2 · Project into Q, K, V: q⁽ⁱ⁾=x⁽ⁱ⁾W_q, k⁽ⁱ⁾=x⁽ⁱ⁾W_k, v⁽ⁱ⁾=x⁽ⁱ⁾W_v
These three W matrices are the only learned weights — and the same three are reused for all six tokens.
Note: dₖ = 2 here (3→2) just to keep boxes readable; real LLMs split d_model across heads, each with a smaller dₖ.
Step 3 · Calc attention scores · Scaled dot product: ω₂ᵢ = (q⁽²⁾ · k⁽ⁱ⁾) / √dₖ
The query now dots each key (not raw x·x); dividing by √dₖ keeps scores stable as dₖ grows.

g.text: Why divide by √dₖ (the book adds it but doesn’t say why): as dₖ grows, the dot products grow in
magnitude, pushing softmax toward near-0 / near-1 outputs where gradients get tiny. Dividing by √dₖ
keeps the score variance ≈ 1, so training stays stable.

svg.text: Step 4 · Calc attention weights · Softmax: α₂ᵢ = softmax(ω₂)ᵢ
Exponentiate each score, divide by the total. Weights are positive and sum to 1.
Weighted sum, the way the code does it: z⁽²⁾ = Σ α₂ᵢ · v⁽ⁱ⁾
Same loop as before, but each pass adds a scaled value vector v⁽ⁱ⁾ (dₖ=2 here), not the raw input.
Bidirectional attention: “journey” attends to all tokens, even later ones — fine when the whole sentence is known.
GPT predicts the next word, so a causal mask zeroes future tokens — each sees only itself and earlier ones.

g.text: for i, v_i in enumerate(values): # values, not raw inputs

svg.text: ↑ after the last += , this is z⁽²⁾
Extension · What a GPT block adds: causal masking + dropout
Now over all tokens as 6×6 matrices (rows = query, cols = key). Mask before softmax; dropout after.
Step 3.1 · Causal mask — between Step 3 (scores) and Step 4 (softmax)
masked_fill (from book): where the boolean mask (triu, diagonal=1) = 1, overwrite that score with −∞.

g.text: Why −∞? e^(−∞)=0, so masked cells vanish in the softmax; each row still sums to 1. (0 fails: e⁰=1.)

svg.text: rows = query x⁽¹⁾…x⁽⁶⁾ (top→bottom), cols = key x⁽¹⁾…x⁽⁶⁾ (left→right)
→ softmax each row ⇒ lower-triangular causal weights (shown below). Row 2 = [0.45, 0.55, 0, …].
(Equivalent to adding a 0 / −∞ mask, as the original Transformer and some code do — same masked scores.)
Step 4.1 · Dropout — between Step 4 (weights) and Step 5 (weighted sum)
Training only: here p=0.5 → zero ~50% of weights at random, then scale survivors ×1/(1−0.5)=2.
×2 compensates so the total stays the same. Real models use smaller rates: p=0.1 or 0.2 → ×1.11 or ×1.25.
input = the causal weights from Step 3.1 (upper triangle already 0, so masking there changes nothing)
At inference dropout is off → weights pass straight through unchanged.
